title: Tractable stochastic analysis in high dimensions via robust optimization
contribution: Proposes replacing the primitives of probability theory by uncertainty sets built from limit laws, so that queueing-network analysis, budget-constrained multi-item auction design and multi-asset option pricing become linear, bilinear or mixed-integer optimization problems, with closed-form robust queue bounds, a robust optimal mechanism and simulation-checked accuracy (a programme survey of six working papers).
problem_entry: {RO+SD+AP} Probability theory was not developed with computational tractability as an objective in high dimension, leaving queueing networks with general distributions, budgeted multi-item auctions, network information theory and multi-asset options open; entry: replace the Kolmogorov axioms and random variables by uncertainty sets from limit laws (abstract p. 1; pp. 3, 5).
key_idea: Assume the conclusions of probability (CLT, stable laws, Shannon typical sets) as set constraints and compute performance as a max or min over the set: closed-form worst-case waiting times, set families closed under network operations (a robust Burke theorem), IC/IR/budget constraints as a robust LP mechanism, options as LPs (pp. 5-10, 12-18, 26-29, 36).
assumptions: Gamma of 2 or 3 fitted empirically (p. 5); queue sets valid for k up to k0, typically n - 30, with equal tail indices (p. 11); RQNA's service-variability parameter fitted by linear regression to simulated single queues (p. 19); polyhedral valuation sets (p. 26); most proofs deferred to working papers (p. 4).
proof_devices: Lindley recursion plus set bounds reduce the worst-case waiting time to a one-dimensional concave maximization with a closed-form, Kingman-like solution (Theorem 2, eqs. 17-25, pp. 12-14)
Robust analogue of Burke's theorem: departure, superposition and thinning sets keep the same form, so a network decomposes node by node (Theorems 3-4, Propositions 2-3, pp. 14-18)
Shannon typical sets as distribution-specific uncertainty sets (Proposition 1, Corollary 1, pp. 8-10)
Auction design as a robust LP with its dual (eqs. 37-43, pp. 26-27); extreme-point optimality of the bilinear subproblems and a generalized Benders decomposition (Proposition 4, Algorithm 4, p. 30)
experiments: RQNA vs Whitt's QNA and simulation on Kuehn's nine-queue network (RQNA within ±3.9%, QNA 5.8-23.7%; Table 1, p. 20) and random 10-30-node networks (below 6.2% with feedback, below 8.5% with mixed arrival laws; pp. 21-22); ROM-Si vs Myerson by simulated revenue under misspecification (+27% to +103% for a wrong family, -17.6% to -58% for a larger true mean; pp. 33-35); option tables repeat S171's numbers (p. 45); no solver, machine or run time reported.
positioning: Against probability's primitives and the simulation or approximation route (QNA) for queues, Myerson and the probabilistic and adversarial auction literatures, and Black-Scholes and DP-based epsilon-arbitrage for options; Kingman and Dantzig quoted as authorities (pp. 3-4, 18, 23-25, 36).
writing: Opens with a history of probability from Pascal and Fermat to Kolmogorov (p. 2); first-person contentions ('In our opinion', 'It is our contention', pp. 3, 45); a survey of working papers with proofs deferred (p. 4).
limits_future: Proofs left to working papers (p. 4); auction results mixed when the mean is misspecified (p. 35); largest option errors for American puts (p. 45); future: the programme should reveal new optimization problems (p. 46).

method_links.note: queueing, auction design and option pricing, owned by probability, economics and finance, written as LP or bilinear programs over uncertainty sets; the auction LP dualized; boundary printed (bilinear subproblems NP-hard for general sets)
presented as a research programme, carried by Bandi with Youssef and Chen in six working papers within two years
why-now argued historically (probability built for foundations, optimization for computation, practical rather than polynomial efficiency as the test) without a measured solver figure
the knob Gamma is fitted to data or, in RQNA, to simulation; no protection-cost curve; probability re-enters through limit laws and calibration (Tension T3)

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: uncertainty sets from the CLT, stable laws and Shannon typical sets replace distributions, and performance becomes a max or min over the set; the same move prices options in S171 (p. 3)

transferable: Turn a probabilistic performance question into a max or min over a set built from a limit theorem, then check that the robust answer has the classical bound's functional form (Kingman) (pp. 5-6, 13-14).
For networks, prove that the set family is closed under the network operations (passing through a node, superposition, thinning), so the network decomposes into single nodes (pp. 14-18).
Write incentive constraints (IC, IR, budget feasibility) as robust constraints over the valuation set and dualize once (pp. 26-27).

Test robustness to misspecification twice: fix mean and standard deviation and swap the distribution family, then sweep the total variation distance, and report where the robust design loses (Tables 7-9, Fig. 2, pp. 33-35).

quotes.text: The key building block in our approach is that rather than assuming as primitives the axioms of probability theory (Kolmogorov axioms and the notion of a random variable), we assume as primitives the conclusions of probability theory, namely its limit laws.
Modeling stochastic phenomena with probability theory is a choice, that is probability distributions are not inherent to the problem.

title: An integer optimization approach to associative classification
contribution: Builds interpretable decision-list classifiers (ORC) from two MIOs, one mining rules on a support-coverage frontier and one ranking them for regularized training accuracy, and reports test accuracy on par with SVMs, trees and ensembles on 11 data sets, with the solver stopped before certifying optimality.
problem_entry: {ML+IO} Accurate classifiers such as SVMs are not interpretable and interpretable trees are not optimized for accuracy; rule learning faces a combinatorial explosion of rules and L! rule orders, which associative classifiers handle heuristically (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: RuleGen mines rules on the frontier of maximal support and minimal coverage, which holds the optimum of many interestingness measures; a ranking MIO orders rules into a decision list maximizing regularized accuracy and learns the default class through two null rules (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: Binary transaction data and binary classes (multi-class extension called trivial); 0-1 accuracy objective; regularization weights chosen so they never trade accuracy; minimum coverage 0.05 and five iterations per frontier point (pp. 2, 6-7).
proof_devices: Continuous x_i forced to 0/1 by constraints (1)-(2), leaving only d binaries (p. 3)
Coverage upper bound lowered step by step plus no-good cuts (6) to enumerate all frontier rules (p. 4)
Ranking MIO with assignment variables and big-M-type links; constraints (11), (12) and (23) added only to tighten the LP relaxation (p. 6)
experiments: 11 data sets (UCI, Crime1-2, Titanic), 3-fold CV against logistic regression, SVM, CART, C4.5, random forests and AdaBoost (R 2.15.0); ORC in AMPL 11.210 with Gurobi; ranking times up to 21,505.7 s, solver generally stopped before optimality, no gaps; highest or tied-highest test accuracy on 4 of 11 sets and lowest on SPECT (Tables 4-5, p. 7); nine-rule Tic-Tac-Toe list against 21- and 36-leaf trees (p. 8).
positioning: Against heuristic rule miners and associative classifiers (Apriori, CBA, CMAR, CPAR), vote-based models such as LAD, and decision lists ordered by interestingness measures (p. 2); claims to be among the first MIO approaches in machine learning (p. 8).
writing: One thesis, no forced accuracy-interpretability trade-off, stated in the introduction and again in the conclusion (pp. 2, 8); supplementary results deferred to a longer DSpace version (p. 2).
limits_future: More computation (p. 2); rankings not certified (p. 7); interpretability subjective (p. 1); future: optimization-based rule mining, interpretable classifiers and new regularizers (p. 8).

method_links.note: rule mining and decision-list learning, owned by data-mining heuristics, written exactly as MIOs; formulation strength named as the key to solvability, LP-tightening constraints flagged

joint MIO replaces heuristic mining and measure-based ordering and duels six standard classifiers out of sample, but without warm starts and without certificates or gaps; early termination defended (Tension T1)
why-now asserted as two decades of MIO hardware and software progress, with no figure
interpretability gets two knobs, set so that they never cost accuracy; a no-trade-off claim instead of a priced curve

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: One frontier for a family of criteria
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: many interestingness measures are monotone in support and coverage, so the support-coverage frontier contains each measure's best rule and is mined once

transferable: When a family of scores is monotone in two primitive statistics, trace their efficient frontier once (bound one, maximize the other, add no-good cuts for ties) instead of optimizing each score (pp. 3-4).
Keep binary only the structural choices; let indicators that the constraints force to 0/1 stay continuous (p. 3).
Add redundant valid inequalities that tighten the LP relaxation, and say which constraints are redundant (p. 6).
Show interpretability on a data set whose true rule people know (Tic-Tac-Toe's three in a row), next to the model sizes of the interpretable competitors (p. 8).

quotes.text: Our ability to solve an MIO problem depends critically on the strength of the formulation, which is related to the geometry of the set of feasible solutions.
We generally terminated the solver before (7) solved to provable optimality.

title: A hybrid approach to beam angle optimization in intensity-modulated radiation therapy
contribution: Optimizes IMRT beam angles over the continuous range together with beam intensities by alternating LP-dual gradient steps and simulated annealing around an exact intensity LP, beating equispaced angles, pure annealing and a candidate-grid MILP on a phantom and one MGH patient (read: article-in-press version).
problem_entry: {HS+LO+AP} IMRT planners choose beam angles by experience and intuition and then optimize intensities; published beam-angle methods need a candidate angle set (abstract p. 1; p. 2).
key_idea: Alternate gradient steps, computed from the dual of the intensity LP after Craft, with simulated-annealing moves over continuous angles, solving the intensity LP to optimality for each angle set (pp. 2, 4-5).
assumptions: Co-planar beams; Hong et al.'s clinical model with physician-set bounds and weights; dose matrices every 2 or 5 degrees, linearly interpolated; beamlet model without collimator delivery (pp. 2-4, 6-7).
proof_devices: No convergence analysis; steps shrink tenfold down to a machine-accuracy threshold (p. 4)
Thresholded per-component angle moves (2 degrees, 1 degree, machine minimum) for coarse dose grids (p. 4)
Adaptive simulated-annealing cooling T0 exp(-c l^(1/d)) with Gaussian moves (p. 5)
MILP comparator choosing n of m candidate angles with cardinality and linking constraints (eqs. 15-17, p. 7)
experiments: Phantom (1,192 voxels; 40 runs of 1,800 s, CPLEX 9.0): about 18% better than equispaced angles, gradient descent alone worst, average run 2.4% and worst 4.2% from the best (pp. 6-7); MILP on 36 or 72 candidate angles optimal in 2,236 s or 123,823 s but 5% or 2.8% worse (p. 7); one MGH pancreas case (CPLEX 11.0, 80,000 s): 11.8-20.7% better than equispaced against 7.3-15.3% for pure annealing (Table 2, p. 8); anytime results at 30 min, 1 h and 5 h (Table 4, p. 10).
positioning: Reviews annealing, genetic, gradient, MIP and score-function methods that rely on candidate sets; builds on Craft's LP-duality gradient and Hong et al.'s multicriteria clinical model (pp. 2-4).
writing: Practice-first framing (planners' intuition, trial and error); results as percentage improvements over equispaced angles and annealing; parameters admitted to be the best of several settings tried (pp. 1-2, 5, 8).
limits_future: Case-specific thresholds, no multileaf-collimator implementation, long runs; future: faster runs from several starting sets, direct aperture optimization (pp. 2, 4, 11).

method_links.note: baseline is the planners' own rule, equispaced angles, on a hospital partner's case with physician-set parameters
roles reversed: the heuristic over continuous angles is the method and the exact MILP over a candidate grid is the beaten opponent; no certificate or gap for the heuristic
the LP stays the inner engine and its dual serves as a gradient oracle for an outer nonconvex search, rather than a class-keeping reformulation of the whole problem
the exact model stalls (34 h for 72 candidates), so local search with restarts runs over the structural variables, the angles; simulated annealing as a working tool (Tension T2)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Heuristic outer search over an LP engine
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: continuous design variables moved by dual-based gradients and annealing, each candidate scored by an exact LP solve

transferable: For design variables that enter an LP's data, get the gradient of the LP optimum from its dual solution and the chain rule through the data matrix, and use it inside a local-plus-annealing search (p. 4).
Tie step sizes and stopping thresholds to the actuator's physical resolution, so the search never proposes designs the machine cannot deliver (pp. 4-5).
Price a discretization: solve the exact MILP on candidate grids of increasing resolution to optimality and compare it with the continuous-space method (p. 7).
Report anytime results (30 min, 1 h, 5 h) next to the full run (Table 4, p. 10).
coauthors: Valentina Cacchiani, David Craft, Omid Nohadani

quotes.text: The proposed method presents a main difference from previous works: it does not require to have on input a set of candidate beam angles.
We wish to mention that we tried several different parameter settings, and we describe in the next section the choice that experimentally turns out to be the best one.

title: Learning preferences under noise and loss aversion: An optimization approach
contribution: Learns linear preferences from adaptive pairwise questions with integer flip variables that absorb inconsistent answers, then recommends items by robust or CVaR optimization over the remaining utility set, tested with simulated users on a recipe recommender.
problem_entry: {RO+IO+DA} Preference learning picks one utility although many fit the answers, people answer inconsistently and are loss averse, and adaptive questionnaires suffer from errors in early answers (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Binary flip variables with a cap absorb inconsistent answers; each question is the pair whose hyperplane is nearest the analytic center of the mixed-integer utility set; the remaining set becomes the uncertainty set of a max-min or CVaR recommendation (pp. 4-8).
assumptions: Linear utility on attributes with u in [-1, 1]^n; margin 0.1; at most 10% of answers flipped; CVaR with binaries fixed at their analytic-center values; recommendations by enumeration over items (pp. 3-5, 7).
proof_devices: Big-M flip constraints and big-M slack selection in a log-barrier analytic-center problem solved by Newton's method (eqs. 1a-1o, pp. 4-5)
Robust counterpart not dualizable over a mixed-integer set, hence enumeration over items (p. 7)
Sample CVaR made an LP by dualizing the inner minimization; samples drawn by hit-and-run with polynomial mixing (eqs. 4-5, p. 8)
experiments: Simulated users only: 10 planted utility vectors, 200 runs per user and noise level, 10 questions, 102 recipes with 186 ingredient attributes; mean and CVaR (5%, 20%) of the true rank of the five recommended recipes against Toubia et al.'s analytic center and a self-correcting variant; the robust version is dominated on average but least variable, CVaR best for noise 0.2 to 0.5 (pp. 8-10).
positioning: Joins economics (prospect theory), machine-learning and OR preference learning, multicriteria decision making and marketing's polyhedral adaptive conjoint analysis, claiming one contribution each to RO, marketing and risk modelling (pp. 2-3, 6).
writing: Contribution list (a)-(c) closes the introduction (p. 3); each departure from Toubia et al. is given a reason (p. 6); conclusions hedged ('we would argue', p. 10).
limits_future: Robust version too conservative (p. 7); parameter values representative, not cross-validated (p. 9); no evaluation with real users' answers (pp. 8-9); no future work stated (p. 10).

method_links.note: the CVaR level is a conservatism knob motivated by the Bertsimas-Sim trade-off and the flip cap is a budget on data errors, but there is no solution-independent bound and the curves run over noise, not over the knob
the CVaR recommendation stays an LP by dualizing the inner problem; boundary printed: the max-min over a mixed-integer set is not dualizable, so items are enumerated
recommendations scored by the true rank of what is recommended (a decision metric) against the marketing incumbent, though with simulated users

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: one binary flip per answer with a cap on the number of flips makes the learned set robust to a fixed number of wrong answers, instead of penalizing errors in the objective

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Elicited feasible set as the uncertainty set
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the set of utilities consistent with the answers becomes the uncertainty set of the downstream recommendation instead of a point estimate

transferable: Cap the number of data points allowed to be wrong (sum of flips at most Gamma k) instead of penalizing errors in the objective (p. 5).
Keep the whole set of models consistent with the data and optimize the decision against it, instead of collapsing it to a point estimate (p. 7).
When the robust counterpart is not dualizable, fix the binaries at a reference point, sample the remaining polytope uniformly (hit-and-run) and optimize the sample CVaR as an LP (pp. 7-8).
Evaluate a recommender with planted true utilities and report the mean and the tail (CVaR) of the true rank of what it recommends, across noise levels (pp. 8-10).

quotes.text: this would minimize the number of response errors we assume happen, instead of the number of response errors that actually happen.
Although the robust optimization approach provides a loss averse method, it tends to produce solutions that may be too conservative.

title: An accelerated first-order method for solving SOS relaxations of unconstrained polynomial optimization problems
contribution: Makes an accelerated first-order method practical for SOS relaxations of unconstrained polynomial optimization by exploiting the orthogonality of moment matrices for O(N^2) projections, solving instances about twice as large as SeDuMi's interior-point method can (read: March 2011 preprint).
problem_entry: {CP} SDP relaxations of unconstrained polynomial optimization grow as O(n^m x n^m), so interior-point SOS software is limited by size, and accelerated first-order methods had not been tried on the class (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Run an accelerated first-order method on Lu's squared-distance-to-the-affine-set reformulation over the cone, and make each iteration cheap: orthogonal moment matrices make AA* diagonal and the affine projection O(N^2) instead of O(M^2 N^2) (pp. 6-12).
assumptions: Even degree; p(x) - gamma* assumed SOS, so the relaxation is exact and strong duality holds; planted random instances with a known optimum, dense quartics and 10%-dense sextics (pp. 5, 7, 12-13).
proof_devices: Orthogonality of the basic moment matrices with Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identities (Lemma 1, pp. 8-9)
Closed-form projection onto the affine set from the normal equations (Lemma 2, pp. 9-11)
Bounded divisors for numerical stability (Remark 2, p. 11) and O(N^2) cost per projection (Lemma 3, p. 12)
O(1/epsilon) iteration bound quoted from Auslender-Teboulle and Lu (Theorem 1, p. 7)
experiments: Matlab AFOM against SeDuMi 1.1 on a laptop, SeDuMi's stopping rule adapted, epsilon = 1e-4, gap to the planted optimum: AFOM reaches n = 30 (quartics) and n = 16 (sextics) where the interior-point method fails beyond n = 15 and n = 9 for memory; interior-point faster on small n and slightly more accurate on quartics; AFOM more variable (Tables 1-2, Fig. 3, pp. 12-17).
positioning: Against interior-point SOS tools (GloptiPoly, SOSTOOLS, SeDuMi), within first-order conic methods (Nesterov, Auslender-Teboulle, Lu, Lan-Lu-Monteiro, Jarre-Rendl); concedes that Newton-CG augmented-Lagrangian methods reach n = 100 with high precision (pp. 2, 6, 19).
writing: Modest abstract ('promising', 'a curious observation'); lemma-proof structure; an unexplained phenomenon reported as unexplained (pp. 1, 17-19).
limits_future: Unconstrained problems with exact SOS relaxations only; synthetic instances; the faster convergence of the second iterate sequence unexplained; future: a first-order warm phase followed by a low-memory second-order method (pp. 5, 12-13, 18-19).

method_links.note: the algorithm, not the model, is redesigned: SDP structure exploited inside a first-order method, a co-authored counter-example to the skill's remark that his record treats solvers as black boxes
reopening rests on a tool change (accelerated first-order methods) and is shown at about twice the interior-point scale, without a quantified speed-up figure
negative results stay in the body: interior-point faster on small instances and more accurate on quartics, AFOM's variability, an unexplained phenomenon, a competitor at n = 100

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Choose the reformulation by measured convergence, not worst-case complexity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: scheme (2.14) chosen over (2.15), which worst-case analysis prefers, because it converged faster on this class; the same practical-tractability stance appears in S065 (p. 4) and S178 (p. 5)

transferable: Before running a first-order method on an SDP, check whether the constraint matrices have disjoint supports; if so, AA* is diagonal and the affine projection is closed-form (pp. 8-12).
Plant the optimum: build test instances as sums of squares around a random point, so the exact optimal value, and hence the true gap, is known (pp. 12-13).
Against an interior-point code, reuse its stopping rule and state in which direction your adaptation is more conservative (pp. 13-14).
Plot histograms of time and gap across instances, not only medians (Fig. 3, p. 17).
coauthors: Robert M. Freund, Xu Andy Sun

quotes.text: However, when applied to the class of polynomial optimization problems under consideration herein, we have observed that (2.14) converges faster than (2.15), as we look at a converging sequence different from the one in the theoretical analysis
We do not yet have either a satisfactory theoretical or practical explanation of this phenomenon.

title: Measuring quality in diabetes care: an expert-based statistical approach
contribution: Trains a three-variable logistic regression on a physician's quality ratings of 101 diabetes patients' claims records to flag poor care for case management (86% accuracy, 95% specificity), validated on 30 hold-out patients and against a second physician.
problem_entry: {AP+ML} Flag individual diabetes patients receiving poor care from insurance claims, in near real time, so that case managers can intervene; claims are the only scalable source and guidelines miss patients with several conditions (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Train a statistical model on a physician's holistic quality ratings of claims records instead of defining quality; some variables come from the physician's written rationales (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: 101 randomly sampled insured diabetics aged 35-55 with two-year costs of $10-20k, low guideline scores over-sampled; binary label poor versus average-or-good; 30 hold-out patients rated by two physicians (pp. 2-3).
proof_devices: n/a (no theory): forward stepwise logistic regression stopped by a bias-adjusted 500-trial bootstrap estimate of out-of-sample accuracy (p. 3)
experiments: 86% in-sample (84% bootstrap) accuracy, sensitivity 54%, specificity 95%, against 78% for the all-good rule and a guideline-only model (pp. 3-4); hold-out 80% against a 63% baseline (p. 5); 67% agreement with a second physician, who fully agrees with the first on 12 of 30 patients (pp. 5-6); worked case-management example: 295 of 1,000 patients flagged, 92% of them with poor care (p. 6).
positioning: Separates its intervention-oriented, patient-level aim from quality studies of health systems, plans, physicians and pay-for-performance; contrasts expert ratings with guideline-based process measures (pp. 1-2).
writing: Clinical-journal register; a credit-card fraud analogy separates identifying poor care from defining it (p. 2); specific limitation paragraphs (pp. 6-7).
limits_future: Two raters, small sample, insured high-cost 35-55-year-olds only, insensitive to low-cost patients; future: a panel of reviewers and refitting on case managers' ratings (pp. 6-7).

method_links.note: judged by its user's decision (the case manager's enriched list, 92% against 50%) and against the current rules (all-good, guideline-only); no field test
variables chosen by greedy forward stepwise selection, the trial-and-error step his later MIO work replaces; Bertsimas's stated role was conception, design and drafting help
the data asset is built first (131 rated patients with narratives), with a plan to grow it from case managers' ratings

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Imitate an expert, test against a second expert
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the model is trained on one physician's holistic ratings, and an independent second physician rates the hold-out set to measure how rater-specific the model is

transferable: When a target resists definition, label a sample with an expert's holistic rating plus a written rationale, and turn recurring rationales into features (pp. 2-3).
Have an independent second expert rate the hold-out set, and report model-expert and expert-expert agreement side by side (pp. 5-6).
Translate sensitivity and specificity into the user's workload: the share of flagged cases that truly need action (p. 6).

quotes.text: Identifying poor care is not equivalent to defining it.
DB participated in the conception and design of the study and helped to draft the manuscript.

title: Robust option pricing
contribution: Prices European, Asian, lookback, American and multi-asset options by robust LPs that minimize the worst-case l1 replication error over CLT-based polyhedral return sets, with a strike-dependent implied risk-aversion parameter that fits market prices.
problem_entry: {RO+AP+LO} Black-Scholes lacks closed forms for American and barrier options, simulation and DP scale badly with dimension, geometric Brownian motion is empirically violated and frictions rule out exact replication (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Polyhedral CLT-type sets on returns replace the stochastic process; the price is the initial value of the self-financing portfolio that minimizes the worst-case l1 replication error, an LP after dualization; American puts hedged against every exercise date, correlation through a D-norm set (pp. 2-7).
assumptions: Discrete time, i.i.d. returns for the CLT set, Gamma as risk aversion (2 for about 95%), inputs from historical means and variances; implied Gamma(K) quadratic in moneyness fitted on training strikes; Proposition 6.1 needs unrestricted positions (pp. 3, 7-8, 10).
proof_devices: Split the uncertainty set at the payoff kink and dualize each piece (Bertsimas-Sim) to obtain an LP with 16T+4 variables and 4T+4 constraints (pp. 4-5)
Robust put-call parity within the two replication errors (Theorem 2.2, p. 4)
Buy-and-hold optimality without position limits and closed-form deep-in-the-money prices for Gamma in an interval (Propositions 6.1-6.3, p. 7; proofs in the online supplement, not in the file)
D-norm written as an LP by duality to keep correlated multi-asset sets polyhedral (p. 7)
experiments: Fits to market prices: MSFT 18-week European calls (errors at most 0.018), MSFT 25-week American puts (up to 0.225; a cubic Gamma(K) cuts replication errors by about half) and 8-week DJIA index calls (Tables 2-5, pp. 9-11); average out-of-sample errors 11.2-15.3% for Asian, lookback and Asian-index options (p. 11); 50-500 assets in at most three minutes (Tables 7-9, p. 11); no competing method, solver, machine or data dates.
positioning: Extends Bertsimas-Kogan-Lo epsilon-arbitrage (l2 to l1) with Bertsimas-Sim duality; against Black-Scholes, stochastic-volatility and jump models, simulation and DP; explains the volatility smile by option writers' risk aversion, citing Taylor's critique of stochastic volatility (pp. 1-2, 8).
writing: Contributions organized as two labelled advantages, tractability and flexibility (p. 2); modelling choices framed 'in our view' (pp. 1-2); results reported as fits to market prices (pp. 9-12).
limits_future: Largest errors for American puts from the worst-case exercise layer; Proposition 6.1 fails under position limits; no future work stated (pp. 7, 12).

method_links.note: pricing, owned by stochastic calculus and dynamic programming, written as LPs whose size grows polynomially; error norm and correlation norm chosen to keep them linear
Gamma is the knob, but it is read off market prices as an implied risk aversion per strike, a data-calibrated knob, with no protection-versus-cost curve

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: CLT behaviour assumed to hold deterministically, giving a polyhedral return set (with S065 pp. 5-10)
the robustness parameter is inverted from each observed option price, as with implied volatility, and fitted as a quadratic in moneyness to price other strikes

transferable: Choose the error norm and the set's norm so that the robust counterpart stays linear (l1 replication error with polyhedral sets; a D-norm instead of l2 for correlation) (pp. 2, 7).
Handle a piecewise-linear payoff inside a robust constraint by splitting the uncertainty set at the kink and dualizing each piece (pp. 4-5).
Calibrate a robustness parameter like implied volatility: invert it per instrument, fit a low-order curve in a market variable, and test it on held-out instruments (pp. 8, 10-11).

quotes.text: Fitting a specific stochastic process to the data is, in our view, a model of reality, not reality itself.
We, therefore, assume as a primitive that this CLT type of behavior happens deterministically.

title: Least quantile regression via modern optimization
contribution: Solves least quantile (and least median) of squares regression to provable optimality with an SOS-1 MIO warm-started by difference-of-convex first-order and sequential LO heuristics, proves existence and breakdown results without general position, and beats the MASS implementation up to n = 10,000 (read: arXiv v2 reprint).
problem_entry: {ML+IO} Least median and least quantile of squares have the maximal breakdown point but are NP-hard, exact algorithms stop near n = 50, p = 5, and heuristics give no certificates (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: An exact MIO with q binary indicators and SOS-1 constraints, warm-started by difference-of-convex first-order and sequential LO heuristics; the MIO also yields existence and breakdown theorems for arbitrary data (pp. 7-21, 25).
assumptions: Linear regression with intercept and no general-position assumption; synthetic contaminated data after Rousseeuw-Driessen up to n = 10,001, p = 20; real robustbase data sets Alcohol, HBK and NOx (pp. 17, 22, 26, 29).
proof_devices: SOS-1 constraints replace big-M to avoid a weak formulation (pp. 8-9)
Order statistic as a difference of convex sums of the largest residuals, each an LP by duality (pp. 10-11)
Majorization argument for monotone descent and an O(1/K) stationarity rate (Theorem 3.1, pp. 13-15)

MIO characterization as a proof device: LQS equals the best Chebyshev fit over q-subsets (Theorem 4.1, p. 18), residual equalities (Theorem 4.2, p. 20), breakdown point (n-q+1)/n of the optimal value (Theorem 4.3, pp. 20-21)
experiments: MATLAB R2011a and Gurobi, 8 cores, 32 GB; relative accuracy to the best solution found, over 20 instances: warm-started MIO best (0-0.13%) against MASS at 9.7-105% (moderate) and 52-147% (large), cold-started MIO 233-418% at scale (Tables 2-3, pp. 25, 31); NOx (n = 8,088): warm MIO best in 1.5-1.8 h, Algorithm 3 within 0.14-0.39% in 6-7 min (p. 31); certified optima for n = 100-500 within two hours, none at n = 10,000 (pp. 6, 32).
positioning: Reviews three decades of LMS algorithms (PROGRESS, Steele-Steiger, Stromberg, Agullo, Hawkins, Erickson et al., Giloni-Padberg) and related robust estimators; generalizes Rousseeuw's and Stromberg's results by dropping general position (pp. 3-5, 17-18).
writing: Abstract leads with global optimality and the early-termination guarantee, leaving the n = 10,000 certificate caveat to the contributions and the conclusions (pp. 1, 6, 32); tractability redefined explicitly as practical solve time (p. 5).
limits_future: No certificate at n = 10,000 within two hours and slowly rising lower bounds (pp. 6, 26, 32); polyhedral constraints on the coefficients offered as an extension (pp. 5-6, 32).

transferable: Replace big-M links by SOS-1 constraints when the big-M variables sit at their bounds and weaken the relaxation (p. 8).
Write an order statistic as a difference of two convex sums of the largest terms, each an LP by duality, and run sequential LO from first-order solutions (pp. 10-16).
Add a box around the heuristic solution to speed up the lower bound, and state that the certified optimum is then optimal within the box (pp. 27-29).
Score methods by relative accuracy to the best solution any method found, averaged over random instances, and show bound-evolution plots with and without warm starts (pp. 24, 27, 30).

quotes.text: Our view of computational tractability is not polynomial time solution times as these do not exist for the LQS problem unless P = NP.
For problems of this size, the MIO algorithm does not provide a certificate of optimality in a reasonable amount of time.
